sources.title: Show HN: Latch – Make any website usable by AI agents in one line (WebMCP)
sources.text: GA4 + Stripe client_reference_id pass-through. Mirror of inkurate's attribution.js. Reads ?ref=/utm_source, stores the FIRST-touch channel in localStorage (latch_ref), mirrors it into GA4 (ref_visit event + channel user property), and appends it as client_reference_id to the buy.stripe.com Pro link so a paid checkout is attributable (read back via `scripts/stripe.py revenue`). Skips any link that already carries a client_reference_id so the dashboard's project-key passthrough is never clobbered. Pure client-side; runs on DOMContentLoaded so the JS-set Pro CTA href is already in place. Slug sanitised to [a-z0-9-] (NOT [a-z0-9_.-]): this first-touch value is later read on /app and appended to the license-key checkout as " __ch_ ". Stripe's client_reference_id allows only alphanumeric/-/_, so a dot is dropped (corrupting the whole reference and breaking the paid customer's key unlock) and an underscore collides with the "__ch_" webhook delimiter. Keep in lockstep with the [a-z0-9-] sanitiser used elsewhere in index.html (#ref capture) and server/app.html. --> Latch — one line of code makes your site work inside AI browsers 🔗 "> 🔗 Latch . How it works Agent's-eye view WebMCP guide Pricing Analytics GitHub WebMCP · W3C standard · Chrome 149 origin trial · Edge 147 · Atlas · Comet One line makes your site work inside AI browsers. AI agents are already clicking through your site — and failing on your buttons and forms. Latch exposes your search, cart, and contact forms as WebMCP tools an agent can actually use. No server. No rewrite. <script src = "https://latch.tools/latch.js" defer ></script> Copy Drop it before </body> . Zero dependencies · ~6 KB · degrades silently where WebMCP isn't present. What Latch does It reads your page (read-only) and registers the actions an agent needs — nothing else. 🔎 search_site Finds your search box, types the query, and submits — so an agent can look things up. 🛒 add_to_cart Detects "Add to cart / Buy now" controls and clicks them on the agent's behalf. ✉️ submit_form Maps your contact / booking / signup fields into a tool an agent can fill and send. 🧭 navigate Surfaces your main nav links so an agent can move around the site reliably. 🛡️ Safe by default Read-only discovery. If WebMCP isn't there, Latch does nothing and never breaks your page. ⚡ Zero backend One static script. No MCP server to host, no API keys, no build step. Agent's-eye view — live This page runs Latch on itself . Below is exactly what an AI agent now sees. Try the demo search and contact form — they're real, and Latch turned them into tools. detecting… Scanning the page… Demo surface (so there's something to detect) Send message Pricing The script is free and open source forever. Pay only if you want the hosted dashboard that shows what agents actually do on your site. Open source Free €0 / forever The one-line script — all WebMCP tools Self-host or load from latch.tools Opt-in analytics, last 14 days Tool calls, success rate & recent feed Create a project key → Hosted control plane Pro €19 / month · per project Everything in Free, plus: 90-day history Per-agent breakdown (which AI browsers) Full event feed & weekly email summary Priority support Upgrade to Pro → Install free first — Pro shows your agent traffic, so upgrade from your dashboard once agents start visiting. Analytics is opt-in and metadata-only : add data-key to your script tag and Latch reports tool name, outcome, and page path — never form contents, query strings, or PII. No key, and Latch makes zero network calls. Questions? Send us a message Tell us what you need — we read every message and reply by email. Send message Guides: WebMCP guide · WebMCP for Shopify · WebMCP for WordPress 🔗 Latch — make your site agent-ready in one line. Open source (MIT) · github.com/r0bertini/latch "Latch" is a common word used by other companies in unrelated classes; this is an independent open-source WebMCP dev tool.

post.title: Make a small site easier for AI agents to use
post.promise: Try Latch on a demo page and review the actions it exposes.
post.whatItIs: Latch is an open-source WebMCP script that can expose a site's search, cart, contact or booking form actions as tools for an AI agent. A beginner's small experiment could install it on a test page and inspect the discovered actions; that student adaptation is hypothetical.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: a small website operator might pay for Latch's hosted dashboard if they want its opt-in agent activity analytics. The source lists a Pro plan at €19 per month per project; it does not establish customer demand.
loop: Add the provided script to a test site's page.
Let Latch inspect the page and register supported actions when WebMCP is available.
Use a test agent request such as searching for a sample item; the hypothetical output is a search result returned through the exposed search action.
Review the registered action and its result manually; a person must approve any purchase or form submission.
post.evidence: Latch's site describes a one-line static script that exposes search, cart and contact or booking form actions as WebMCP tools, with no backend. It says the script is open source and offers an optional hosted analytics dashboard. The described demo includes a search and contact form.
post.uncertainty: The source describes product capabilities but provides no independent usage or customer evidence. WebMCP availability varies; the site says Latch does nothing when it is unavailable. An exposed form or cart action can have consequences, so review inputs and results before submission or purchase. A beginner's test setup is a proposal, not an established customer workflow.
first24Hours: Create a disposable test page with a search field and contact form.
Add Latch's script and check which actions it detects in a supported browser.
Try a harmless sample search and manually inspect the result before enabling any send or purchase action.

ease.reason: The site says installation is one static script with no backend or build step, though a beginner still needs a test page and compatible browser.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: site operators might pay for the listed hosted dashboard, but the source gives no evidence of buyers or demand.

feasibility.reason: A test page can exercise the documented search action, while WebMCP availability and consequential form or cart actions need care.

autonomy.reason: The script can discover and register actions, but a person must review form submissions and purchases.

evidence.reason: The first-party site describes the working demo and product actions but supplies no independently documented real-use evidence.

post.title: Test agent-ready tools on a small website
post.promise: Try a one-page script that lets an AI agent find and use a few site controls.
post.whatItIs: Latch says its free, open-source script exposes search, navigation, cart, and contact-form actions to AI agents through WebMCP, a browser tool interface. A student could test a tiny version on a personal demo site, using Latch as a reference. That student project is hypothetical.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: a small business that wants its website to work with AI agents might pay for setup or monitoring; the source does not establish customer demand.
loop: Choose a test page and list the controls an agent may use.
Add a script that exposes only those controls as tools.
Ask an agent to search or navigate the test page.
Review each action and check that forms are not submitted without approval.
Record tool name and outcome locally, then inspect the results by hand.
post.evidence: Latch's site describes a free open-source script that registers search, cart, contact-form, and navigation tools, and says it uses read-only page discovery. It describes opt-in analytics as metadata-only. Source: https://latch.tools
post.uncertainty: The source describes Latch's product, not independent results or buyer demand. A student build would need to limit available actions and require a person to review purchases and form submissions; browser support for WebMCP may vary.
first24Hours: Make a demo page with a search box and a navigation link.
Read the Latch guide and identify which actions are safe to test.
Try one agent search and manually verify the page and resulting action.

ease.reason: A beginner can start on a demo page; adding a script and testing agent actions still requires basic web skills.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: a small business might pay for setup or monitoring, but the source gives no evidence of buyers or demand.

feasibility.reason: A limited test of search and navigation fits a four-week project; broader site actions and browser support add uncertainty.

autonomy.reason: The described script registers repeatable page actions, while a person must set boundaries and review consequential form or cart actions.

evidence.reason: The first-party site describes a working live demo and the script's actions, but supplies no independent use evidence here.

post.title: Try a local dictation and meeting-notes workflow
post.promise: See how sideOS describes dictation, meeting summaries and review points.
post.whatItIs: sideOS is a Mac assistant whose site describes on-device dictation and meeting transcription, plus summaries and action items. A beginner could try a short, non-sensitive recording and check the transcript and summary; this test adaptation is hypothetical.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: an individual Mac user may pay for the app's listed lifetime licence. The source lists a one-time price of $89.90 but does not establish buyer demand or sales.
loop: Start dictation or manually choose to record a meeting; the site says recording is offered and does not start on its own.
For the hypothetical test, use a short sample recording with consent from everyone involved.
Let the app transcribe the audio on the Mac and draft a summary and action items.
A person checks names, wording and action items against the recording before sharing or creating reminders.
Choose whether to keep or delete the audio using the app's retention setting.
post.evidence: The product site describes dictation using macOS speech engines and says meeting transcription runs on-device. It says a call window prompts the user to record, then the app produces a transcript, summary and actions; action items can become reminders. It lists a $89.90 one-time licence.
post.uncertainty: These are first-party product claims; the attached page does not establish accuracy or independent customer use. A person should obtain recording consent, verify names and decisions, and approve any reminder or shared summary. The short sample workflow is a hypothetical test, and performance may depend on macOS and the audio.
first24Hours: Check that you have a compatible Mac and choose a non-sensitive short audio sample.
If recording other people, ask for their consent before starting; otherwise use your own sample speech.
Compare the generated transcript and summary with the audio, correcting errors before using any action items.

ease.reason: The source describes a simple dictation gesture and meeting prompt, but the experiment requires a compatible Mac and careful handling of recordings.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: Mac users might buy the listed lifetime licence, but the source supplies no customer or sales evidence.

feasibility.reason: A short recording can demonstrate the described transcription and summary loop, though Mac access, consent and transcript review are required.

evidence.reason: The first-party site provides detailed feature descriptions and demonstrations, but no independent evidence of actual customer use.

post.title: Test a self-hosted media library idea
post.promise: Explore whether creators want to keep media on hardware they control.
post.whatItIs: Shotstash's repository describes it as a self-hosted media cloud for creators. A student could interview a few creators and sketch a small, local media-library workflow without claiming that Shotstash provides any specific organizing or AI feature. This proposed experiment is hypothetical.
post.whoPays: Hypothesis: creators who want media hosted on their own hardware might pay for a setup or support service; the source does not show that they will.
loop: Ask a creator what media they keep and where they store it.
Record only the storage needs they choose to share.
Sketch a simple library workflow for files on hardware they control.
Have the creator review whether the sketch matches their needs.
Do not move or upload any files without explicit permission.
post.evidence: The GitHub repository identifies Shotstash as a self-hosted media cloud for creators. Its repository page also shows an MIT license. Source: https://github.com/Aldyernesto/shotstash
post.uncertainty: The attached source excerpt establishes the project's description but not its detailed features, working behavior, or creator demand. The proposed interview and sketch are hypothetical; a person must control any file access or hosting decisions.
first24Hours: Read the repository description and note what it does and does not establish.
Draft five neutral questions about creators' media storage needs.
Ask one creator for an interview, without requesting access to files.

ease.reason: A beginner can start with interviews and a sketch, but the source gives too little detail to build against specific features.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: creators might pay for setup or support, but neither a buyer nor a concrete purchasing need is evidenced.

feasibility.reason: Interviews and a workflow sketch fit four weeks; implementing a useful product cannot be scoped from this brief source excerpt.

autonomy.reason: The attached description does not establish an automatable loop; the proposed discovery and review work is manual.

evidence.reason: The repository establishes a named project and its self-hosted media-cloud purpose, but the excerpt provides no working demonstration details.

B.refusal: The attached repository page identifies Shotstash as a self-hosted media cloud for creators and shows repository metadata, but provides no usable product workflow or demonstration evidence from which to write a beginner post without inventing capabilities.
